commentary.bottom_line: The listed tests, all level 4 studies in offline or simulated settings, suggest that asking a language model for a target grade level often lowers readability scores, though outputs frequently remain above the target and some simplifications lose accuracy. No listed test measured whether patients or caregivers in care settings found, understood, or acted on information more reliably, and the one test reporting a knowledge outcome found technical wording associated with better scores among 71 college students.

perspectives.view: All listed tests are level 4 studies in offline or simulated settings, and most use readability formulas as a surrogate for comprehension. Some added clinician or lay raters, but none tested patients in care. In one study of 71 college students, technical responses were more likely in the high knowledge-gain group (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41). Indirectness and inconsistency support very low certainty.

Simplification may trade accuracy for readability. In one study, the lowest-grade prompt reduced accuracy scores from a median of 5.0 to 4.0. Another reported expert-rated inaccuracy of 19.0% versus 28.6%, a difference that was not statistically significant (p=0.47). A third study found that eighth-grade translations gave the best balance of accuracy and readability.

Prompted Spanish materials scored better than standard handouts on seven readability measures, but no patients read them. In real deployments, 982 AI-generated visit summaries had a mean FKGL of 9.3, and chatbot responses in a trial including patients with limited English proficiency averaged an 11th-12th grade level. These hazard studies did not test a fix.

The FDA draft guidance says materials should suit the intended audience's reading level but names no metric or grade. The listed studies used sixth-, seventh-, and eighth-grade targets and several different formulas. This variation may make it hard to show that a product meets the guidance.

commentary.research_gap: No listed study tested reading-level-matched materials with intended users in real workflows. Such studies would need to measure comprehension, time to find key information, correct action, and errors, with accuracy checked against the original text. Studies also need to establish which readability metric and target grade best predict understanding for each user group and task.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests targeted materials toward low health literacy and one assessed Spanish-language materials, but these were text analyses with no patient readers. A hazard study included patients with limited English proficiency, but it did not test the practice. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users, so benefit for these groups remains unverified.
